title: Summary Writing: Answering Exactly What Is Asked

blocks.text: A candidate writes six beautiful sentences about a passage on flooding. She scores two marks out of five. The rubric had asked for three effects of the flood; she wrote about its causes. In the summary section, elegance counts for nothing if you have answered a question nobody asked.

blocks.markdown:
Summary tests two skills at once:

1. **Selection** — picking out the ideas the rubric asks for and rejecting everything else.
2. **Re-expression** — stating each idea briefly, accurately and in your own words.

Marks are awarded per point, so the whole task turns on identifying the right points. Fine writing cannot rescue a wrong selection.

blocks.title: The rubric is the question
blocks.text: "In three sentences, one for each, state three effects of the flood" tells you the subject (effects, not causes), the number (three) and the form (three separate sentences). Underline all three requirements before you read the passage again.

blocks.markdown:
### What is never a summary point

A passage is mostly padding around a small number of ideas. Reject:

- **Illustrations and examples** — signalled by *for instance*, *for example*, *such as*, *consider the case of*
- **Statistics and anecdotes** used to support a point already made
- **Repetition and restatement** — signalled by *in other words*, *to put it another way*, *that is to say*
- **Rhetorical questions** and direct quotations
- **Your own opinion**, which has no place in a summary at all

What remains is the skeleton of the argument, and those bones are your points.

blocks.title: Producing a one-sentence summary answer
blocks.prompt: Rubric: In one sentence, state one reason rural clinics fail. Passage: "Rural clinics fail for reasons that have little to do with money. Drugs arrive but there is no cold chain to keep them usable. Nurses are posted but no accommodation is built for them, so they commute and arrive late. Equipment is delivered but nobody is trained to maintain it."

steps.text: Read the rubric first. It asks for ONE reason, in ONE sentence. Anything more is wasted.
Identify the general claim and set it aside. 'Reasons that have little to do with money' is the topic sentence, not a reason itself.
List the candidate reasons: no cold chain for the drugs; no accommodation, causing late arrival; no trained maintenance staff.
Choose one and check it really answers the rubric. Take the cold chain: it explains a failure and is not an example of something else.
Re-express it in your own words. 'No cold chain to keep them usable' becomes 'the clinics lack the refrigeration needed to store medicines properly'.
Write it as one complete sentence with a subject and finite verb: 'Medicines spoil because the clinics lack the refrigeration needed to store them properly.'
Check for lifting. No phrase of four or more consecutive words has been copied, so the expression marks are safe.

blocks.answer: Medicines spoil because the clinics lack the refrigeration needed to store them properly.

items: Read the rubric and underline the subject, the number of points and the required form.
Read the passage, marking only the sentences that answer that subject.
Cross out illustrations, statistics, repetitions and rhetorical questions.
Group any sentences that make the same point and count them as one.
Write each point as a complete sentence, in your own words, in the order the rubric implies.
Reread each sentence to confirm it stands alone and contains no lifted phrase.

rows: Shows no understanding, so expression marks are lost
Rewrite the idea using different vocabulary
The points are not the ones the rubric asked for
Underline the rubric's key noun before reading
Only the first ones are marked; extras are wasted or displace correct points
Count your sentences against the rubric
A phrase is not a sentence, so it forfeits expression marks
Give every point a subject and a finite verb
A summary reports the writer's ideas, not yours
Delete every *I think* and *in my view*
Look for *for instance* and skip that sentence
blocks.caption: The six faults that lose most summary marks

blocks.title: Four consecutive words is the danger line
blocks.text: As a working rule, if four or more words appear in your answer in the same order as in the passage, you have lifted. Technical terms and proper names are unavoidable, but ordinary phrasing must be your own.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: Write each summary point as a numbered sentence on a fresh line, exactly matching the number asked for. This makes it impossible for the examiner to miss a point, and it forces you to check that you have produced the right quantity.

points: Summary tests selection of the right ideas and re-expression in your own words.
The rubric fixes the subject, the number of points and the form of the answer.
Illustrations, statistics, repetitions and opinions are never summary points.
Sentences that restate one another count as a single point.
Write each point as one complete sentence, and produce exactly the number requested.
Avoid copying four or more consecutive words from the passage.
